description: I’m a 19-year-old student interested in how machine learning can help solve problems in astronomy. My current projects focus on gravitational lensing and exoplanet detection methods.
summary:
Waypoint searches the entire planet for the places most similar to three real Mars sites: Gale Crater (Curiosity), Jezero Crater (Perseverance) and Arcadia Planitia, a candidate site for a future human base. 
NASA’s GLDAS dataset (2014 annual averages on a 1° global grid) was used to describe every patch of land on Earth by surface temperature, rainfall, snow depth and soil temperature at a depth of 1-2 meters (as a proxy for permafrost). Because Mars is far colder than anywhere on Earth, each feature was ranked from 0 to 1 across Earth’s land, and each Mars site was placed on that same scale. A weighted similarity search then scored every location, and a random forest trained on known analog sites provided a second, data-driven view. 
Without having the analog sites as input, the method ranked the Atacama Desert in the top 0.4% of Earth’s land for Gale Crater and Devon Island in the top 1.5% for Arcadia Planitia. Lesser-known candidates were also identified in Xinjiang, the Namib Desert and northern Greenland.
details:
What it does: Waypoint searches Earth’s land for the places most similar to three Mars sites: Gale Crater (Curiosity), Jezero Crater (Perseverance) and Arcadia Planitia, a candidate site for a future human base because of its shallow buried ice. Instead of relying on hand-picked analog sites, every 1° patch of land (about 110 × 110 km) is scored for how well it matches each Mars environment.

How it works: Four variables from NASA’s GLDAS land model (2014 annual averages, accessed through NASA Giovanni) describe each location: surface temperature, rainfall, snow depth and soil temperature at 100-200 cm depth (as a proxy for permafrost).

Because Mars is far colder than anywhere on Earth, each feature is ranked from 0 to 1 across Earth’s land, and each Mars site is placed on the same scale. A weighted similarity search then scores every location. A random forest trained on eight known analog sites adds a data-driven check, tested with leave-one-out validation. K-means and PCA group Earth’s environments and show where the Mars sites fall among them.

Results and impact: The known analogs were not used as input to the similarity search, yet the Atacama Desert ranked in the top 0.4% of Earth’s land for Gale Crater and Devon Island in the top 1.5% for Arcadia Planitia. Lesser-known candidates were found in Xinjiang, the Namibian Desert, northern Greenland and Baffin Island. Other high-scoring regions are visible on the maps, and the full ranked list of candidates is available in the GitHub repository. This makes analog site selection repeatable and data-driven, and the same method can be applied to other targets, such as the Moon.

Tools: Python (NumPy, pandas, xarray, scikit-learn, matplotlib) and NASA Giovanni. Runs on a standard personal laptop in about 15 seconds.

Limitations: 1° resolution, one year of data, climate-only features (so geology-based analogs score low), no data south of 60°S, and only seven labeled analogs.
